It is clearly known that these are not form (*rūpa*).

Furthermore, in the *Tattvasiddhi*, while elucidating the meaning of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), it initiates the discussion by stating "the category of knowledge of the six supernormal powers" (*ṣaḍabhijñājñānavarga*).
If this were the case, then while the nature of four of the powers would be knowledge (*jñāna*), two of the powers would not be.

That [text] should have designated it as "The Chapter on the Wisdom of the Fourfold Supernormal Powers" (catur-ṛddhi-vidyā-paṭala). Why, then, does it say "The Chapter on the Wisdom of the Sixfold Supernormal Powers" (ṣad-abhijñā-vidyā-paṭala)?
Furthermore, within the *Avataṃsaka*, the six supernormal powers are further divided into ten clarities (daśa-vidyā).
The ten clarities (*daśa-vyākaraṇāni*) are wisdom (*jñāna*).
How can it be said that two of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are form (*rūpa*)?
Furthermore, the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) says:
The fourfold penetration is called knowledge;
the divine eye is called vision.
Regarding the fourfold penetration as knowledge:
The [supernormal powers] are the body, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, and recollection of past lives.
Since that treatise states that the divine ear is a form of knowledge (jñāna),
it is clear that the essential nature of the supernormal power of the divine ear is not matter (rūpa).
As it is with the divine ear,
so it is with the divine eye; however,
in that treatise, "seeing" is designated by the name of the function of the eye’s illumination.
The essence of this treatise is wisdom;
therefore, the sutra names it the "supernormal power of knowledge regarding birth and death.
This concludes the first section, which analyzes [the subject] in terms of form and so forth.
Next, regarding the second section, which distinguishes the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) in relation to the six consciousnesses (ṣadvijñāna),
there are differing opinions among the commentators.
If one follows the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā):
The two supernormal powers of the eye and ear have as their essence the mental factor of wisdom associated with the visual and auditory consciousnesses,
because these two powers function externally while in meditative concentration.
The remaining four supernormal powers have as their essence the mental factor of wisdom associated with the mental consciousness.
Because it functions as excellent concentration (*samādhi*),
and because in that school all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) exist simultaneously,
it is taught that its essence consists of the associated factor of wisdom (*prajñā-saṃprayukta*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
all six supernormal powers (abhijñā) have as their essential nature the wisdom within the mental states of the sixth consciousness;
in that school's tenet, the five sensory consciousnesses possess no wisdom whatsoever.
Therefore, it is not taught that wisdom within the five consciousnesses constitutes its essence.
Furthermore, since in that school all minds and mental factors arise sequentially and separately,
it is not taught that associated wisdom serves as the universal essence.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles are mostly explained in accordance with the Abhidharma,
as it is also taught therein that mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) arise simultaneously with the mind.
It is taught that the supernormal powers (abhijñā) attained by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas all have wisdom associated with the mental consciousness as their substance.
Since this wisdom of reality-as-it-is (yathābhūta-jñāna) constitutes the essential nature of these powers, these two sections are concluded.
Next, the third section provides an analysis based on the eleven knowledges.
As for these eleven knowledges,
they consist of the ten knowledges together with the knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
This is the eleventh.
What are the ten knowledges?
They are the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path; these constitute four.
When the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are added to the preceding, there are six.
Among these, the four knowledges of the Truths pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are termed the knowledge of phenomena;
those pertaining to the two higher realms are termed subsequent knowledge.
When the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are added to the preceding, there are eight.

These two, which follow the six aforementioned knowledges, are designated as the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising when they pertain to the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*).
These eight knowledges are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
The ninth, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), is exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The tenth, the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), is both with and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Such are the ten knowledges.
This meaning has been fully and extensively analyzed in the preceding chapter on the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).
As for "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūtajñāna*),
it is that which Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess, free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
He thoroughly knows all phenomena;
he knows them as they truly are,
rather than claiming to know what he does not know.
Therefore, it is called "knowledge as-it-is" (yathābhūta-jñāna).
As for its essential nature,
it is as explained in the *Bhūmivastu* (Dichijing):
This refers to pure knowledge, omniscience, and unimpeded knowledge.
These have been extensively explained and analyzed as previously presented in the chapter on the three types of knowledge.
Now, based on this knowledge, the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) are distinguished.
The six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) of the Hīnayāna are subsumed within the ten knowledges (daśajñāna);
the six supernormal powers of the Mahāyāna are subsumed within the knowledge of suchness (yathābhūtajñāna).
The six supernormal powers of the Hīnayāna are subsumed within the ten knowledges.
What are their characteristics?
As stated in the Abhidharma:
they are the supernormal power of the body, the divine eye, the divine ear, and the recollection of past lives.
These four types of supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) possess the nature of one single wisdom,
because they are exclusively contaminated (sāsrava).
The supernormal knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), however, possesses the nature of all five wisdoms.
If one knows another’s mind that is with outflows (sāsrava), it is of the nature of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
If one knows another’s mind that is without outflows (anāsrava), it is of the nature of the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
Knowledge of the untainted minds of others in the desire realm is of the nature of dharma-knowledge;
knowledge of the untainted minds of others in the higher realms is of the nature of subsequent knowledge;
and knowledge that knows both the higher and the lower is of the nature of the knowledge of the paths.
Knowing both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) is a knowledge that universally pertains to the minds of others.
Therefore, the knowledge of others' minds possesses the nature of five knowledges. Question:
Regarding the knowledge of the untainted minds of others,
for what reason is it termed the nature of the knowledge of the path?
It is because the essential nature of the untainted minds of others is itself the path.
Therefore, we know that this mind is designated as "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*).
If this is so, since the objects known— the contaminated minds of others— are in essence suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*),
why is the knowledge that cognizes them not called "knowledge of suffering" or "knowledge of the origin"?
The commentary states:
It should be equal;
however, the nature of that uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) knowledge of others' minds is subtle.
This resembles the depth and shallowness of that Truth of the Path.
One who knows that mind is thus able to know the Path;
therefore, knowing that mind is itself the nature of the knowledge of the Path.
The mental objects associated with outflows and belonging to others are coarse and superficial;
the principles of suffering and its origin are subtle in meaning.
Now, one whose wisdom is coarse cannot reach that which is subtle.
Therefore, one knows that regarding the outflow-tainted mind of another, it cannot be termed the knowledge of suffering or its origin.
This explanation is coarse and resembles the subtle, yet it is still not exhaustive;
one must further investigate with subtlety.
Question: One who knows another’s untainted mind—does this mean they know the objects of that other’s untainted mind?
Or does it mean they know the path and its traces upon the basis of that other’s untainted mind, according to the fourfold principle of universal application?
The commentary states:
"Correct discourse" refers to knowing the mental affairs of others;
if one were to know the principle, it would be so.
Since principles interpenetrate one another without distinction between self and other,
how can it be called "knowledge of others' minds"?
[The interlocutor] asks:
If this knowledge of others' minds does not take principles as its object,
the treatise itself judges it:
"Although it dispels darkness regarding the sixteen aspects, it is not untainted (anāsrava)."
How is it that this is called "knowledge of the path"?
The explanation states:
This meaning is indeed difficult and not easily understood.
There must be some news.
To speak precisely, when one knows another's mind through this notification, it is neither untainted (*anāsrava*) nor the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
In that treatise, those termed "untainted" (anāsrava) are so called because they are proximate to the untainted and resemble the untainted;
furthermore, they are proximate to the untainted.
Because it explains the beginning and the end in their entirety, it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, it is described as "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*);
because it is proximate to the Path and resembles the contemplation of the Path, it is said to be "endowed with the knowledge of the path."
Furthermore, that which is proximate to the Path—
expounded from beginning to end— is called "possessing the knowledge of the Path.
What is the meaning of this?

Whenever one wishes to know another’s untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), one must first contemplate that path as being like a track, according to the principle of its general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
Only then can one subsequently infer and know that other's mind based upon it.
Therefore, it is called "knowledge of the path" (mārgajñāna) by way of explaining its general characteristics throughout from beginning to end;
it is called "untainted" (anāsrava).
To distinguish the beginning from the end, this [initial stage] is not untainted.
Nor is it the knowledge of the path.
[The opponent] asks:
Why must one first contemplate the principle (li) if one wishes to know the untainted mental affairs of others?
Thereafter, one ascends to discern the minds of others;
one must not expect to know the affairs of others directly.
The commentary explains:
The Way is like a track; the principle of mounting it proceeds from the stages of *uṣmagata* and so forth.
Through repeated contemplation until it becomes thoroughly matured, one sees the untainted (*anāsrava*) other-mind upon directing the mind toward it—something previously unknown.
Only from the stage of *anāgāmin* upward does one first begin to train in this contemplation.
Generally, one who wishes to know the difficult must begin from the easy.
Therefore, one who wishes to know the untainted (anāsrava) mind of another must first contemplate the principle (li).
Contemplation of the principle is the definitive proximate cause for that [knowledge].
Therefore, it is explained generally as being "endowed with the knowledge of the path. A question is asked: [Why is this so?]
If one knows that the knowledge of others' minds when they are untainted (anāsrava) must first contemplate the principle (dharma),
and is called "knowledge of the path" (mārgajñāna) because it proceeds from proximate application,
then the knowledge of tainted (sāsrava) minds should likewise be understood in this way.
Why can it not be termed "knowledge of the origin of suffering" based on its proximate means?
The explanation is that they are not analogous.
Within that state of outflow-free concentration (*anāsrava*), the contemplation of principle (*yuanli guan*) comes first,
and the knowledge of the mind (*zhixin*) follows later;
the former is easy and the latter is difficult.
Therefore, one first contemplates the principles and only thereafter knows the mind.
Among those with outflows (*sāsrava*), ordinary persons have from the beginning frequently known the minds of others;
yet at the time they were so knowing, they had not yet contemplated suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).
Therefore, one does not enter [the path] by means of the contemplation of the origin of suffering.
Because one does not enter [in this way], it cannot be said that one possesses the full knowledge of the origin of suffering.
Furthermore, the outflow-tainted mind of another is originally known through repeated cognition.
If one already knows it, it is easy.

However, since the principle of the origin of suffering (duḥkha-samudaya) has not been seen from the outset, but is only now being studied through contemplation starting from the stage of "warmth" (uṣmagata),
it is difficult to know.
That which is easily known does not rely on that which is difficult to know as a skillful means.
Since the contemplation of suffering and its origin is not their proximate cause,
it cannot be generally designated as the "knowledge of suffering and its origin."
This view is indeed correct.
Even if there were alternative interpretations, they would all be considered difficulties;
such is the case regarding the knowledge of others' minds.
The knowledge subsumed within the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayābhijñā) is not fixed;
it may consist of six, eight, or all ten knowledges.
If the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows is defined as the "knowledge of the destruction of the outflows" (āsravakṣayajñāna), it then has the nature of six knowledges.
These are the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of phenomena, inferential knowledge, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and conventional knowledge.
To know the cessation of the desire realm is called the knowledge of phenomena;
to know the cessation of the higher realms is called inferential knowledge.
Knowing the higher and knowing the lower are collectively termed the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
When one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) contemplates cessation, it is called the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣaya-anutpāda-jñāna*).
When a mind with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*) takes this as its object, it is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Excluding the knowledge of suffering, origin, the path, and the knowledge of others' minds,

because these do not constitute the exhaustion [of outflows]. If that noble person’s noble wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) can exhaust all outflows, it is called the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna), and its nature consists of eight knowledges.

Because conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and so forth cannot ultimately exhaust the fetters (*saṃyojana*), conventional knowledge is excluded;
furthermore, those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have ceased seeking and do not infer the minds of others. Therefore, [these] are excluded.
Excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the remaining eight are all capable of bringing the fetters to ultimate exhaustion;
therefore, one possesses these eight knowledges. Question:
How can the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) attain ultimate exhaustion of the fetters and be said to possess the complete knowledge of phenomena?
The commentary states:
Because the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation and the path within the desire realm can sever the higher fetters and bring about the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
If one were to explain that the attainment of the name "one whose outflows are exhausted" constitutes the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows, it would consist of ten types of knowledge;
such is the case in the Hīnayāna.
In the Mahāyāna, however, it is subsumed under the knowledge of reality as it is (yathābhūtajñāna).
What are their characteristics?
Those first five supernormal powers are all subsumed under omniscience (*sarvajñā*) and unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Within the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows is designated as the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
These are also subsumed under omniscience (*sarvajñā*) and unimpeded knowledge (*asaṅgajñāna*).
If one realizes the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), it is categorized as the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*) and pure knowledge (*viśuddhajñāna*).
Such is the analysis according to these various knowledges; thus concludes this section on the three gateways.
Next, the fourth section distinguishes the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) in relation to the ten clarities (daśavidyā).
The ten clarities are as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
where it explains that the six supernormal powers constitute the ten clarities.
Therefore, it is necessary to define and distinguish the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
What are their characteristics? Regarding the power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*):
He says that the supernormal knowledge of others' minds and the supernormal power of recollecting past lives constitute a single clarity of mind.
He states that the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives constitutes one clear knowledge,
while each of the remaining four is divided into two.
The supernormal power of the body is twofold:
first, the clear wisdom of the power of fearlessness through which one dwells securely,
transforming with mastery and coming and going without obstruction throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The second is called the Wisdom-Light of the Variegated Form Body (*vicitra-rūpa-kāya-jñānāloka*),
which is able to manifest the various distinctions of all bodies.
The divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is divided into two parts.
First, the clarity of the wisdom of the divine eye,
which illuminates and perceives present forms and images with distinct clarity;
second, the clarity of the wisdom that extends to the end of all future kalpas.
One thoroughly understands death here and rebirth there in the future.
The divine ear is twofold:
first, the clear knowledge of the divine ear.
First, the ability to hear distant sounds.
Second, the immeasurable wisdom-light of various sounds,
which understands the distinctions among the languages and voices of all sentient beings.
The section on the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya) is divided into two parts. First, the clarity of knowledge in accordance with reality:
by realizing the true nature of phenomena, one is able to exhaust all outflows.
Second is the wisdom and clarity of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), through which one thoroughly understands the dharma of extinction in the three vehicles.
Having thus concluded these four gates, they are distinguished according to the ten clarities (*daśa-vidyā*).
Next, the fifth section distinguishes the six supernormal powers (abhijñā) in relation to the two types of liberation.
Regarding the "two liberations":
the first is liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
Second, liberation of mind.
The Sūtra states that there are two kinds of liberation;
one meaning is as follows:
The liberation of the mind is defined as the mastery of a concentrated mind through the severing of the fetter of craving;
the liberation by wisdom is defined as unimpeded wisdom through the eradication of ignorance.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
Severing delusion through the light of wisdom,
removing the heart of craving to attain liberation—
thus did Vimalakīrti proclaim.
The eternal extinction of delusion and craving gives rise to clarity and liberation;
this also applies to this gateway.
Within this gateway, all six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) are subsumed under the liberation through wisdom (prajñā-vimukti).
Because of wisdom,
the liberation of the mind is the basis for the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā);
it is the cause of the six supernormal powers, not their actual essence.
Regarding the second meaning, as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
by severing all innate fetters and afflictions, the true mind emerges from its obstructions; this is called the liberation of the mind.
That text states:
"Greed, hatred, and delusion are forever severed and extinguished;
because they are extinguished, it is called liberation of the mind."
Thus, one should know that the severance of the fetters of inherent nature and the afflictions constitutes the liberation of the mind.
Furthermore, that text states:
"The intrinsic nature of this mind is not conjoined with greed, hatred, or delusion."
For example, although the sun and moon may be obscured by smoke, clouds, dust, or mist, they do not become fused with those five types of obscurations.
Because they are not so fused, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have eternally destroyed craving; this is called the liberation of the mind.
Therefore, it is known that when the true mind emerges from the afflictive hindrances, it is called "liberation of mind" (*cittavimukti*).
When ignorance regarding phenomena is severed and one perceives all dharmas without obstruction, it is called "liberation through wisdom" (*prajñāvimukti*).
Thus, the text states:
Unimpeded knowledge regarding all phenomena is called liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
Within this framework, the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) are subsumed under these two types of liberation.
What is the manner of their inclusion?
The former five supernormal powers are subsumed under wisdom-liberation (*prajñā-vimukti*).
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"By means of wisdom-liberation, that which was previously unheard is now heard."
That which was previously unseen is now seen;
that which was previously unattained is now attained.
One should also say:
That which was previously unknown is now known;
though the text is concise and does not analyze this further,
that one hears what was not heard before is the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*).
To see what was previously unseen is the supernormal power of the divine eye;
to reach what was previously unreachable is the supernormal power of the body;
and to know what was previously unknown is the pair of supernormal powers regarding others' minds and past lives.
Within the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), there are two aspects combined in meaning:
first, the exhaustion of one's own outflows is termed the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows and is subsumed under the liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*);
second, knowing the exhaustion of others' outflows is termed the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows and is subsumed under the liberation by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
Such is its essential nature.
Next, three sections clarify the meaning of attaining the six supernormal powers through cultivation.
There are two types of attainment.
First, attainment through detachment;
second, attainment through skillful means.

When one abandons the desires of the lower realms and attains the higher dhyānas, the supernormal powers (abhijñā) that depend upon those dhyānas are attained at that very moment; this is called "attainment through detachment."
That which is attained through the cultivation of skillful means is called "attainment through skillful means.
According to the Abhidharma, among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the single power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is attained solely through the abandonment of desire.
The divine eye and divine ear are obtained solely through skillful means (*upāya*).
As for the remaining three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), they are obtained both through the abandonment of desire (*vairāgya*) and through skillful means.
Why, then, is the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*) obtained only through the abandonment of desire?
The state where all fetters are exhausted is the untainted noble virtue;
since this is itself supernormal power,
it is thus proclaimed.
The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) regarding one's own realization of their exhaustion is attained solely through the abandonment of desire (*vairāgya*).

However, if one knows the exhaustion or non-exhaustion of outflows in others, it constitutes the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows; this must be accomplished through the supernormal power of reading the minds of others (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*) by means of skillful application.
For now, following one interpretation,
I shall omit further discussion.
Why is it that the two supernormal powers of the divine eye and the divine ear are acquired solely through preparatory effort (*prayoga*)?
The Abhidharma proclaims that the two supernormal powers of the eye and ear are by nature indeterminate (avyākṛta);
their functioning occurs outside of meditative concentration and does not coexist with it.
When one abandons lower desires and attains higher meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this supernormal power (*abhijñā*) is not obtained;
for this reason, it is not attained through the mere abandonment of desire.
Only after attaining concentration and subsequently practicing specific skillful means does one finally obtain it.
For this reason, it is obtained solely through application (*prayoga*).
Why, then, are the other three also obtained through detachment (*vairāgya*) as well as through application?
Because their nature is wholesome and they coexist with a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*).
When one abandons lower desire and attains higher concentration, one obtains it immediately; thus, it is obtained through the abandonment of desire.
Although it is indeed obtained at the time of abandoning lower desire, [it is specifically characterized by the attainment of the higher state].
It can only be accomplished but does not manifest before one;
it cannot be used in the present. One must further apply skillful means (upāya) to obtain its manifestation for use.
Therefore, it is obtained through skillful means.
Just as wealth located in another place, though it belongs to oneself, cannot be used immediately,
but can only be used once one employs a means to go and retrieve it,
so too is that [the storehouse consciousness].
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, the single supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is obtained solely through the abandonment of desire,
which is the same as in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
The remaining five supernormal powers are obtained solely through preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Why is this so? Because that school proclaims that all meritorious qualities are only termed "attained" once they have been cultivated and achieved such that they are accomplished and no longer lost.
There is no dharma that has not yet been cultivated or manifested which can be pre-emptively termed "attained.
For this reason, when one is separated from the lower desires, the five supernormal powers, such as the power of the body (*ṛddhi-vidhi*), are not yet termed "attained."
It is attained only after cultivation;
therefore, it is attained through skillful means.
According to the Mahāyāna, the exhaustion of outflows realized by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas themselves is called the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).
Only those attained through the abandonment of desire.
Knowledge of the exhaustion of others' outflows and the remaining five supernormal powers are attained both through the abandonment of desire and through application. Why is this so?
The six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) of the Mahāyāna take wisdom according to reality (yathābhūta-prajñā) as their essence.
That essence is itself meditative concentration (samādhi).

When one internally realizes the cessation (nirvāṇa) by severing and detaching from the afflictions (kleśa) through concentration according to reality, one immediately attains those supernormal powers of concentration.
Therefore, it is attained through the separation from desire.
At the time of initial cultivation, through the application of skillful means (*upāya*), the functions [of the mind] arise accordingly, perfuming and stimulating the true mind;
thus, it is attained through skillful means.
How is it known that the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) of the Mahāyāna are all accompanied by meditative concentration (samādhi)?
As Vimalakīrti says:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, always abide in samādhi and clearly perceive all Buddha-lands."
It is not by means of dualistic characteristics.
As it is with the divine eye,
so it is with the remaining supernormal powers.
Therefore, they are all immediately in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Because they are immediately in meditative concentration, they all attain freedom from desire.
[The interlocutor] asks:
Regarding "attaining the exhaustion of outflows through detachment from desire":
from the detachment of which stage does one attain the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows? To explain:
There are three distinctions:
first, distinguishing the end from the beginning;
second, departing from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to attain the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).
Because one has not yet exhausted the outflows by merely becoming detached from the desires of the lower stages.
Second, this refers to the inclusion of the beginning by means of the end;
that is, after one has already severed and become detached from the desires of the single stage of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception.

In the lower stages, the untainted antidotes all increase and become more luminous; collectively, these are subsumed as the supernormal power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-abhijñā*).
Third, regarding the general discussion according to their respective portions:
within the various stages, the untainted [attainments] obtained through the partial abandonment of desire are all the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* proclaims that bodhisattvas possess the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*).
A question is asked:
"The exhaustion of outflows is attained through the abandonment of desire (*vairāgya*)."

It is for the sake of abandoning the desires of the lower realms to obtain the superior qualities of the higher; for the sake of abandoning the desires of the higher realms to obtain the qualities of the lower;
and for the sake of abandoning the desires of one's own level to obtain the qualities of that same level.
The commentary states:
This meaning is also present. How so?
Just as one who severs the fetters of desire attains the untainted merit (*anāsrava-guṇa*) of the stage of the first dhyāna—
whereby all such cases are termed "severing lower desire and attaining superior merit"— so too,

by severing the fetters from the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one attains the superior portion of untainted merit belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna.
All such cases are termed "severing the higher desires to obtain the merit of the lower [stages].
What is the untainted (anāsrava) excellence of the first dhyāna?
According to the Abhidharma, the untainted first dhyāna can sever the fetters (saṃyojana) from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is stated that the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna of the Mahāyāna can sever all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms.

Within this antidote, that which can sever the delusions from the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is termed the "superior portion" (*viśeṣabhāga*) of the untainted first dhyāna.
This untainted state must first be attained by severing the fetters of the higher realms;
it cannot be obtained prior to that.
By severing the fetters of the first dhyāna, one likewise attains the untainted merit of the first dhyāna.
This is called abandoning the afflictions of one's own stage and attaining the virtues of that same stage.
This applies to all such cases.
It is asked:
Regarding those who attain through the departure from all desire: will they attain dharmas already previously attained,
or will they attain those not yet previously attained?
If one were to obtain only those untainted virtues previously attained, then at the time of becoming free from desire,
one would not obtain those that have never been attained before. However, if one attains both [the previously attained and] those not previously attained, [then it is logical].
In that case, ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) should attain the untainted (*anāsrava*) state at the time they abandon desire;
and Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas should attain all the merits of the first dhyāna at the time they abandon desire.
If one were to fully attain these, one would be identical to all Buddhas;
the same applies to the other stages.
Thus it is explained.
That which is obtained through the departure from desire is not fixed;
some may obtain only those dharmas previously attained.
Ordinary persons who have originally attained various dhyānas subsequently obtain the merits arising from those dhyānas.
At times, one may regress and give rise to afflictions of a lower stage, thereby losing superior qualities; subsequently,
by severing the fetters of the lower stage, one regains the dharmas previously lost,
yet does not attain the untainted (anāsrava).
This is because ordinary beings lack the skillful means to incline toward untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
Consequently, some may attain through penetration that which was previously unattained;
likewise, when a noble one (*ārya*) severs the fetters of a lower stage, they simultaneously attain the untainted merits of a higher stage.
Because there are preliminary expedient means for such inclinations,
even when these are attained, they each have their own limits and cannot exceed those bounds.
Because these minor sages cannot be equated with the Buddha,
what is the meaning of this?
For now, let us explain it by way of the first dhyāna.
The remaining categories may be understood accordingly.
Within the stage of the first dhyāna, there are immeasurable distinctions among the classes of untainted (anāsrava) merits;
therein are contained the virtues of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.
For those who practice the preparatory means before they have abandoned desire according to their respective capacities,
they will attain it immediately after abandoning desire;
for those who lack such means, it is not so.
One does not obtain it by being free from desire.
When a śrāvaka becomes free from desire, they obtain only the untainted merits (anāsrava-guṇa) of a śrāvaka,
but do not obtain the untainted merits of other persons.
All such cases are likewise.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of obstacles to the virtues of the first dhyāna:
first, the obstacle of the lower stage.
The afflictive hindrances of the desire realm obstruct the virtues of the first dhyāna;
those of its own level [the first dhyāna] obstruct [the virtues of] the first dhyāna; and the afflictive hindrances of the first dhyāna obstruct the virtues of the first dhyāna.
Third, the obstacles of the higher stages:
all afflictions from the second dhyāna upward obstruct the merits of the first dhyāna.
Within these lower obstacles, there are immeasurable degrees of coarseness and subtlety.
The Śrāvakas sever the coarse [defilements] and attain the coarse grade of merit within the first dhyāna;
for the Pratyekabuddhas, that which is severed becomes increasingly subtle and that which is attained becomes increasingly superior,
until finally, for the Buddhas, it is severed completely and that which is attained reaches its ultimate limit.
The medium-grade obstacles within one's own stage are likewise immeasurable.
When Śrāvakas eliminate the coarse [obstacles], they attain the medium-grade merit of the first dhyāna;
when Pratyekabuddhas refine it further, what they attain becomes progressively superior.
Only upon reaching Buddhahood is one's inquiry exhausted; only then does what has been attained reach its ultimate limit.
Within the obstacles of the higher stages, those of medium grade are likewise immeasurable.
Each attains its respective result according to the degree to which [defilements] have been abandoned.
As it is with the first dhyāna, so it is for the others.
The same applies to the other dhyānas.
For this reason, although one may attain what was previously unattained through the abandonment of desire, it is not identical to that of a Buddha.
[The interlocutor] asks:
If it is said that the afflictions of the first dhyāna can still obstruct the merits of the first dhyāna,
and that the fetters from the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception can also obstruct the merits of the first dhyāna;
Can the obstacles within the first of the ten bodhisattva stages (bhūmis) also obstruct the virtues of that first stage?
Furthermore, can the obstacles of the second stage up to the Buddha stage also obstruct the virtues of the first stage?
There are points of agreement and difference regarding this explanation. To discuss them according to their differences: the eight dhyānas are the stages where [the path] is acquired through birth.
Within the stage of the first dhyāna, the untainted (anāsrava) states that arise therein are capable of severing all afflictions (kleśa) of the three realms.
The afflictions to be abandoned and their respective means of abandonment are equally characterized by the sense of being obstacles;
the same applies to the remaining dhyānas.
However, the boundaries for the abandonment of obstacles differ across the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The realization of the first stage cannot sever the obstacles pertaining to the second stage, nor even the obstacles of the Buddha stage.
Because they are not severed,
the obstacles belonging to the second stage and so forth do not obstruct the first stage.
The same applies to the other stages.
Just as the realization of the path of seeing and the realization of the path of cultivation constitute distinct, unmixed antidotes,
it was further asked:
The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the locus for attaining the virtue of abandonment, wherein one may sever lower faults and attain the virtues of the higher stages.
Since the eight dhyānas are not a locus for attaining through abandonment,
when one leaves behind the faults of the lower levels, one should not thereby attain the meritorious qualities of the higher dhyānas.
The commentary states:
Pure dhyāna is the locus for attaining abandonment, which is identical to the ten stages (bhūmi).
Therefore, by departing from the desires of the lower realms, one attains the virtues of the higher dhyānas.
The pure [attainment] is the basis for obtaining the untainted;
therefore, the untainted [attainment] produced by relying on a lower dhyāna can sever all afflictions of its own stage as well as those of the higher stages.
When severing those fetters, one attains the untainted (anāsrava) merits of the lower stages;
even if one uses other dhyānas to sever higher afflictions, one likewise attains the untainted merits of the lower stages.
The meaning of "identical" and "not identical" regarding the distinct severances at each stage of the ten stages is as follows.
Discussing them in terms of their identity, the dharmas of the ten stages exist within each individual stage.
The calculations for coarse and subtle particles, as well as their obstructions, are likewise immeasurable.
This is discussed here with reference to the first stage;
the others may be understood by analogy.
In the first stage (*bhūmi*), when the mind is purified of the coarse categories of hindrances, one abandons them and attains the coarse categories of merit within that first stage;
those which are subtle are abandoned at the time of the second stage.
One attains the progressively superior merits within the first bhūmi;
the obstacles belonging to the first bhūmi persist until Buddhahood,
and even the merits attained therein reach their ultimate limit only at Buddhahood.
Because the obstacles of the first stage are abandoned in common with those of all the stages, the obstacles abandoned within each stage are likewise obstacles to the first stage;
the same applies to the remaining stages.
Thus it is proclaimed in the *Avataṃsaka*.
The Bodhisattva’s first stage universally encompasses the merits of all stages;
this is the meaning of this gate.
In terms of its correspondence to the dharma-position, it is identical to the stage of dhyāna.
Question: It was stated previously that the supernormal power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñānābhijñā) is attained through the abandonment of desire (vairāgya).
What is meant by "separation from characteristics"?
This has been fully explained in the preceding chapter on severing the fetters and need not be discussed further here.
Question: The Abhidharma states that the supernormal powers of the body (*kāyābhijñā*) and so forth are also attained through the abandonment of desire.
Is the desire thus abandoned identical to, or distinct from, the obstruction that hinders these supernormal powers?
The explanations differ.
That which is abandoned by him— the defiled afflictions that obstruct supernormal powers—
is the non-defiled ignorance that acts as a dam blocking penetration.
Furthermore, when one attains dhyāna through the abandonment and detachment from desire,

and when the obstructions to the supernormal powers (abhijñā) are severed, one attains only those powers. Moreover, regarding the specific abandonments of desire, one focuses exclusively on the supernormal power of the body, the knowledge of others' minds, and the recollection of past lives.
The obstruction that hinders the supernormal powers (abhijñā) is that which universally obstructs the five supernormal powers.
Furthermore, the attainment of the supernormal powers through the severance of that desire is called "attainment through detachment" (vairāgya-lābha).
The attainment of the supernormal powers through the severance of the obstruction that hinders them is called "attainment through application" (prayoga-lābha).
To distinguish this completely, it is asked:
among the afflictions of the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra-kleśa*), in which abode is this included? There are two interpretations for the explanation.
One is that the coarse is differentiated from the subtle.
These four afflictions of householders and their kin are not the stage of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*).
The stage of the abode of ignorance is not severed by those of the two vehicles (*śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*),
whereas ordinary persons and those of the two vehicles are able to sever the obstructions that block the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Second, subsuming the derivative from the fundamental:
this refers to the non-defiled ignorance within ignorance.
If it were merely ignorance, how could ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles ever be able to sever it?
Learning [the path] accordingly provides a temporary cessation;
however, because one cannot yet achieve permanent separation from it, this is not yet called "abandonment.
Furthermore, it was asked: among the nine stages of the three realms, to which stage does this obstruction belong?
The commentary states:
This obstruction is not the same as the defiled afflictions (kleśa),
for it is definitely restricted to specific stages (bhūmi).
However, the minds that are obstructed by these various stages exist from the desire realm up to the fourth dhyāna;
this is because there are obstructions within these stages,
and furthermore, because they vary in coarseness and subtlety according to those stages.
Question: It was stated previously that the five [supernormal powers], such as the supernormal power of the body and so forth, are all attained through skillful means (*upāya*).
What, then, are these skillful means?
The five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) are cultivated based on the fundamental dhyānas of the mind-faculty;
therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"The five supernormal powers reside in the four fundamental dhyānas and not in other concentrations."
Furthermore, taking the first dhyāna as a basis to clarify the characteristics of cultivating the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*),
the other cases may be understood by analogy.
There are three types of supernormal power cultivated for the supernormal power of the body (*kāyābhijñā*).
First is the path of skillful means:
first entering the fundamental concentration of the first dhyāna;
this is precisely *śamatha*.
Subsequently, one forms the thought of flying back and forth, or the thought of transforming into large or small sizes;
this is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Returning to meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one again forms thoughts of flying back and forth and so forth.
Thus, after many repetitions,
this constitutes the path of skillful means for the supernormal power of the body.
Second is the path of non-obstruction.
Through the power of the preceding preparatory application (*pūrvaprayoga*), one enters meditative absorption and gives rise to wisdom;
first, the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*) severs hindrances and penetrates obstructions;
then, the three paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
Following the path of non-obstruction, one single path of liberation realizes the removal of those hindrances;
from that point onward, whatever one intends to do can be accomplished immediately according to one's prior mental intention.
The supernormal power of the body is likewise.
The cultivation of the supernormal power of reading others' minds also consists of three kinds of paths:
first, the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
One first enters meditative concentration and then observes the minds of others to discern their thoughts;
practicing this repeatedly is called the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*).

Second is the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*). By the power of the preceding preparatory application (*pūrvaprayoga*) which has been cultivated and aroused, one enters meditative concentration and gives rise to wisdom.
This single path of non-obstruction severs the obstacles and clears the blockages, leading to the three paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Following the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga), one realizes the removal of those hindrances through the single path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
Subsequently, when one wishes to know the minds of others, one is able to know them immediately.
The cultivation of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā) likewise involves three types of paths.
First is the path of skillful means:
first one enters meditative concentration,
and subsequently one gives rise to mental visualization.
One recollects events experienced in the past,
tracing them from the most recent to the more distant,
following them in successive order.
He returns to meditative absorption in this manner many times;
these constitute the two paths of non-obstruction.
The three paths of liberation are similar to the preceding ones.
Regarding the cultivation of the supernormal power of the divine eye, according to the Abhidharma, there are only two paths.
First is the path of skillful means:
first, the mind enters meditative absorption;
next, one takes up signs such as the sun, moon, lamps, and light.
Forming the perception of seeing from afar, one re-enters meditative absorption.
In this manner, one repeats the practice many times until it is thoroughly mastered.
This is the second path of non-obstruction.
Through the power of the preparatory application that has been cultivated, one enters meditative absorption and gives rise to wisdom;
by means of the path of non-obstruction, one severs hindrances and penetrates obstructions,
so that upon emerging from concentration at a later time, whatever one wishes to see is immediately seen.
That school asserts that the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is neutral (*avyākṛta*);
therefore, within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there can be no path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
However, according to the *Tattvasiddhi* and the Mahāyāna, the divine eye is wholesome and coexists with the concentrated mind.
For one who practices in this way, there is the path of liberation,
which is the same as in the case of the supernormal power of former lives, the supernormal power of others' minds, and so forth.
Regarding the cultivation of the supernormal power of the divine ear, according to the Abhidharma, there are likewise two paths.
First is the path of skillful means:
first, one enters a state of meditative concentration;
next, one takes up various sounds and forms the perception of hearing them from afar.
He returns to meditative absorption.
In this manner, he repeats it many times until it is thoroughly mastered.
This constitutes the two paths of non-obstruction.
Through the power of the prior preparatory application that has been cultivated and aroused, one enters meditative concentration and gives rise to wisdom.
By means of the path of non-obstruction, one severs hindrances and penetrates blockages;
subsequently, upon emerging from concentration, whatever one wishes to hear is heard immediately.
The path of liberation is not the same as the divine eye;
the *Tattvasiddhi* and the Mahāyāna also have liberation,
which resembles the aforementioned divine eye.
Question: Among the various supernormal powers (abhijñā), there are those obtained through the abandonment of desire (vairāgya-prāpta) and those obtained through skillful means (upāya-prāpta).
Is there a difference in the breadth or scope of these two types of attainment?
There are three types of exegetical explanations.
First, regarding the analytical distinction of the meaning: "attainment through detachment" is narrow, whereas "attainment through skillful means" is broad.
As for those who have abandoned desire,
they merely attain the dharmas previously acquired; however,
the superior and wondrous supernormal powers (abhijñā) never before attained are all brought forth through the cultivation of present skillful means.
Regarding the second meaning:
detachment from desire is broad,
while skillful means are narrow.
As for those who have become free from desire,
they attain all the dharmas that they have previously attained since beginningless time.
As for that skillful means:
it is obtained by those who are able to enter it in the present life;
it is not obtained by those who are unable to enter it.
Regarding the third meaning:
it refers to the equality attained through the skillful means of abandoning desire.
The Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas are all able to manifest entry into whatever has been attained by others through that abandonment of desire.
Cultivation is achieved in this manner.
Next, four sections clarify the meaning of the differences between the Great and Small Vehicles.
There are five such differences.
Their essential natures differ.
All six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) take wisdom as their essence.
In the Śrāvaka vehicle, the six supernormal powers take the mental factor of wisdom within the empirical consciousness (saṃvṛtijñāna) as their essence.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, at the time of initial cultivation, it takes the wisdom-factor within the active consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) as its essence.
Because there are phenomena external to the mind,
mastery over them is termed "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*).
Next, one cultivates by taking the wisdom within that deluded consciousness as the essence.
One perceives that all phenomena arise solely from the mind and that there are no phenomena external to the mind;
thus, one attains unimpeded mastery over the phenomena of one's own mind.
Ultimately, it is accomplished through functioning with true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*) as its essence;
seeing that phenomena are nothing but the True, one attains unimpeded mastery within the reality of one's own essential nature.
Second, the objects of focus differ.
In the Six Supernormal Powers of the Hīnayāna, whatever is performed involves攀緣 (pán-yuán, objective focalization) and discrimination; it cannot be without an object.
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, at the stage of initial cultivation, there is an object of focus.
Next, one cultivates the object of mindfulness of breathing, which cannot be without an object.
Ultimately, it culminates in equanimity and non-objectification, like the sun shining universally without discrimination.
All performed activities are empowered by the power of the Dharma, yet no mental effort is exerted.
Third, there is a difference between the permanent and the impermanent.
The six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) of the Hīnayāna are impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing.
The six supernormal powers of the Mahāyāna are initially impermanent.
It is ultimately true and eternal;
while objects appear to arise and perish, its essence remains forever unchanging.
Thus, the four reliances are certainly not the same [as the four truths].
The six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) of the Hīnayāna rely solely on concentration on phenomena (*vastu-samādhi*);
dwelling the mind upon a phenomenon is what constitutes concentration on phenomena.
The six supernormal powers of the Mahāyāna initially rely on concentration on phenomena.
Next, according to the certainty of principle:
destroying appearances and abiding in emptiness is the certainty of principle;
ultimately, it culminates in the tranquil certainty of the true essence itself.
The nature of the true mind being quiescent is the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Abiding within this concentration, the mind remains unmoving,
and the power of the *samādhi* manifests its function spontaneously.
Furthermore, within the Hīnayāna, the first five supernormal powers arise solely based on the fundamental dhyānas of the four dhyānas.

The single supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya) relies upon the four dhyānas, the preliminary stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), and the three formless attainments (ārūpya).
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, the initial cultivation is the same as that of the Śrāvakas;
ultimately, however, it is perfected by relying on all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), which can give rise to [all attainments].
Furthermore, whatever concentration a Śrāvaka relies upon, [it is the same].
The supernormal powers (abhijñā) manifested by others cannot function when they enter other meditative absorptions (samādhi);
however, it is not so for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Whatever meditative absorption they rely upon to manifest their supernormal powers, those powers are able to function even when they enter other meditative absorptions.
As Nāgārjuna has analyzed,
their functions differ.
Within the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), when the power of the body (kāyābhijñā) is explained in detail, there are ten distinct varieties.
First, there is a difference between ascending and descending.
The supernatural powers manifested by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, relying upon the first dhyāna, reach only as far as the first dhyāna.
One cannot reach the higher [levels].
Because one traverses by means of the earth [element], it is the same for the other meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*);
one merely reaches one's own level and cannot transcend it.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are not like this;
relying on the supernatural powers (ṛddhi) produced from the first dhyāna, they reach all stages (bhūmi),
and it is the same for the other meditative concentrations (samādhi).
Second, there is a difference in breadth and narrowness,
as stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
for a śrāvaka, two thousand lands constitute the range of their pervasive field.
The sphere of activity for a pratyekabuddha extends across three thousand world-systems.
Furthermore, Nāgārjuna states that among the śrāvakas of lesser capacity, those who do not apply focused attention have one thousand world-systems as their sphere of activity.
If one applies mental attention, two thousand lands constitute the range of their perception;
among the great śrāvakas, even those who do not apply mental attention have two thousand lands as the range of their perception.
If one who is a practitioner of mental attention (*manasikāra*) takes the three thousandfold world-system as their sphere of penetration,
among the persons who are pratyekabuddhas there are both great and small;
those small pratyekabuddhas who do not practice mental attention take two thousandfold world-systems as their sphere of penetration.
If one who applies mental attention takes the three thousandfold world system as their sphere of activity,
then a great pratyekabuddha— whether or not they apply mental attention—
always takes the trichiliocosm as their sphere of activity.
These are called "narrow.
Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take all worlds and all realms of sentient beings as their universal sphere of activity,
they are called "broad."
Third, there is a slight difference regarding multiplicity:
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot manifest many forms simultaneously with a single mind,
whereas Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can, at one time, manifest all manner of physical forms throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
At one time, they can manifest bodies within the five destinies;
fourth, their sizes differ,
for the great bodies manifested by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot enter small ones.
Manifested small bodies cannot contain the large;
yet the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest large bodies that fill the trichiliocosm,
and are able to enter a single atom with those large bodies.
They manifest a small body like a minute speck of dust,
yet are able to contain all things within that small body.
Furthermore, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can cause great worldly forms and objects to enter into the small.
The small can contain the large;
the two vehicles cannot.
Fifth, there is a difference in slowness and speed.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas take a long time to reach distant places because they do not possess the supernormal power of psychic travel (ṛddhividhi-jñāna).
Buddhas and bodhisattvas, however, can reach the worlds of the ten directions in a single thought-moment.
Because they have attained the supernormal power of mastery over others' minds (ṛddhividhi), the six realms differ in their reality or unreality.
Whatever manifestations śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas produce are merely similar to the actual objects; they do not possess practical efficacy.
Whatever manifestations Buddhas and Bodhisattvas produce all yield practical utility,
as stated in the *Bhūmivastu*:
there are seven types of differing activities.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas transform immeasurable people,
each causing them to possess a mind;
according to whatever single task they perform, they cause each person to have distinct discernment.
The followers of the Two Vehicles cannot do so.
Eighth, the manifestations differ:
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest only a single body, yet cause people to perceive it differently.
Yet, with a single utterance, they cause others to hear it as something extraordinary;
while remaining securely established in a single land, they manifest themselves simultaneously throughout the ten directions—
something that those of the Two Vehicles cannot achieve.
The functions of the nine faculties differ.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess the mutual functioning of the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*),
whereas those of the Two Vehicles cannot.
The ten masteries differ as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
In all that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do, their physical and mental faculties possess mastery that does not follow one another.
When his body manifests as large, his mind is not large;
when his body manifests as small, his mind is not small;
when his body manifests as joyful, his mind is not joyful.
Although his body manifests sorrow, his mind does not grieve;
all such things as these are beyond the capacity of those of the two vehicles.
The supernormal power of the body is thus.
Within the supernormal power of the divine ear, there are six differences:
first, the difference regarding above and below.
The divine ear attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas based on the first dhyāna hears only sounds from the first dhyāna downward;
it does not hear those above.
The same applies to the other dhyānas;
they do not extend beyond their own respective levels.
Relying on whichever dhyāna they may be in, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas hear all sounds with the divine ear (divya-śrotra) thus obtained.
Second, the difference in breadth and narrowness may be understood by reference to what precedes.
Third, the difference in sudden versus gradual distinction.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas hear various sounds individually and cannot do so simultaneously;
the Buddhas and bodhisattvas hear them all at once and instantaneously.
Fourth, they differ in being coarse or subtle.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
"Even the most subtle sounds, such as those spoken in a whisper, are all heard by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
whereas the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot."
Fifth, there is a difference in speed:
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas hear all sounds as soon as they direct their minds toward them,
whereas those of the Two Vehicles cannot.
Only through the application of many skillful means can one come to hear and know it.
Sixth, there are differences between the real and the unreal;
regarding all sounds, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not err in what they hear.
The two vehicles are not like this;
they may still be subject to error.
Such is the case with the divine ear.
Within the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are seven types of differences.
First, the difference between higher and lower:
according to the Abhidharma (*Vibhāṣā*), there are three kinds of transcendence (*atikrama*) by which one does not know their mind.
First is the transition between persons:
an inferior person does not understand the mind of a superior person.
Second is the transition between faculties.
The dull-witted person does not know the mind that seeks to benefit others.
Third is the stage of the earth (bhūmi):
one who is in a lower meditative stage does not know the minds of those in the meditative concentrations of a higher stage.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is taught only that humans and the faculties can attain supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), but not that the stages (*bhūmi*) can do so.
What the *Tattvasiddhi* teaches is thus conflated with the Mahāyāna;
for in the Mahāyāna, it is taught that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas rely on the lower stages to develop such supernormal powers.
They are also able to know the minds of those in the higher realms;
however, there is a difference in the breadth and narrowness [of their scope].
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas can at most know the minds of sentient beings within a single trichiliocosm.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to know all things.
There are three ways in which their sudden comprehension differs:
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can suddenly and fully comprehend the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings.
The two vehicles cannot [attain this].
Fourth, there is a difference between the coarse and the subtle:
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas only know the coarse minds of ordinary beings and lesser sages, and are unable to reach the subtle.
The subtle objects known by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—
even the minds of Buddhas— they are able to know.
Fifth, there are differences in speed and slowness.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know all mental states as soon as they wish to know them;
the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot do so,
for they must employ many skillful means before they can come to know them.
Sixth, there is a difference between the empty and the real.
What is known by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is unerring;
this is not the case for those of the Two Vehicles.
What is known may be subject to error.
Seventh, there is a difference in temporal divisions:
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas know only the minds of sentient beings in the present.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to know the minds of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
Such is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*). Within the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-abhijñā*), there are ten distinct types.
First, there is a difference between upward and downward vision.
The divine eye attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, regardless of which dhyāna it relies upon, perceives only its own level and cannot reach those above;
however, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas see everything.
Second, they differ in their breadth and narrowness;
third, they differ in their sudden and gradual distinctions.
These may be understood by reference to what preceded.
Fourth, there is a difference in coarseness and subtlety.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas perceive everything down to the most subtle levels, including even the minute particles of matter that border empty space;
the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot do so.
Fifth, they differ in terms of slowness and speed;
sixth, they differ in terms of being empty or real.
These are similar to what was mentioned previously.
Seventh, there are differences in their temporal scope:
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas can see as far back as eighty thousand kalpas into the future,
whereas Buddhas and Bodhisattvas see to the very end of time.
Eighth, the difference between self and others.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas perceive only external forms but do not perceive their own eyes.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to see their own eyes;
there are nine different ways of seeing phenomena,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The divine eye possessed by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is able to see all forms arising and ceasing from moment to moment,
as well as the impure skeletons of oneself and others;
these two vehicles cannot do so.
Tenth is the difference in the faculties (*indriya*).
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas behold the physical forms of people, they immediately know whether their faculties are sharp or dull, great or small.
The two vehicles are incapable [of this].
Such are the differences in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Within the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), there are eight points of difference.
First, there is a difference regarding the upper and lower realms.
Whatever dhyāna stage a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha relies upon to attain the knowledge of past lives,
they know only the past lives of beings within their own level and those of the lower levels.
They cannot know what lies above;
all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know it entirely.
Second, they differ in their breadth and narrowness.
Third, the difference regarding the three meals,
which may be understood by analogy with what preceded.
Fourth, the difference regarding the coarse and the subtle.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know all past events, both great and small,
whereas those of the Two Vehicles cannot;
fifth, their speed differs.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know past events as soon as they resolve their minds upon them;
the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot do so.
Sixth, there is a difference regarding the real and the unreal.
What is known by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is unerring and differs from that of the Two Vehicles;
it is distinguished by its seven temporal phases.
The followers of the two vehicles can know events as far back as eighty thousand kalpas;
however, that which is known by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is infinite.
It is asked:
The Sūtra states:
"The seer Kapila was able to know events of eighty thousand kalpas in the past;
the same was true for the future."
Since śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are both noble ones (ārya),
their knowledge ought to be far-reaching;
why then do they act in the same manner as them?
The commentary states:
This is known by means of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Within the sphere of the conventional, that which is known through the repeated cultivation of sharp faculties is remote.
For those of dull faculties, what is to be known is approached through little practice;
this does not distinguish between ordinary persons and sages.
There are eight different types of mastery.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know their own past lives and the past lives of others,
and they are able to cause others to know their own past lives as well.
It enables others to know their own past lives,
enables others to know the past lives of others,
and even causes those other sentient beings to know one another's past lives in succession.
The two vehicles are incapable [of this].
Such are the differences in their past lives.
Within the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-abhijñā), there exists its specific variety.

First, knowing the exhaustion of others' outflows is called the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*). Second, personally realizing the exhaustion of one's own outflows is called the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
There are seven distinct ways of knowing the exhaustion of others' outflows.
First, there is a difference between the upper and lower realms.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas know only the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya) in their own stage and those below;
they cannot know what is above.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know everything completely.
Second, there is a difference in breadth and narrowness:
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas know the exhaustion of the outflows (āsravakṣaya) of others within a single world-system.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas fully know all things;
these three categories differ in their modes of cognition.
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cognize through specific conditions and cognize only specific objects.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know all things instantaneously and simultaneously.
There are four levels of coarseness and subtlety:
that which is known by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is coarse and shallow.
The knowledge of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is profound and subtle.
There are five [stages] that differ in their slowness or speed;
for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, no expedient means are required.
One who has resolved their mind knows this immediately;
those of the Two Vehicles cannot.
Sixth, there is a difference between the empty and the real.
What is known by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is erroneous;
what is known by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is the reality.
These two differ in seven respects.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas know whether the outflows (*āsrava*) of present sentient beings have been exhausted or not, but they do not know those of the past or future.
Buddhas and bodhisattvas know all of these completely.
Such is the difference in their knowledge of the exhaustion of others' outflows.
There are three differences in the self-realization of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). First, there is the difference in the realization of the Dharma:
the realization of the Dharma by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is coarse and shallow.
They merely realize the emptiness of persons;
the realization of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is profound and deep,
exhausting the understanding of both forms of emptiness.
And they both realize the profoundly deep nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Second, there is a difference in the removal of hindrances:
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas sever only the four abodes of clinging.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas extinguish these at the fifth stage;
their modes of abandoning and grasping differ from those of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, who attain realization by grasping at tranquility.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attain cessation yet do not abide therein;
they attain great nirvana yet do not abandon the world;
though they do not abandon the world, they are eternally in nirvana.
The distinctions between the large and the small are thus.
Next, the five gates provide a classification according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate are these three natures.
Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the single power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is exclusively wholesome by nature.
Regarding the remaining five powers, they are generally said to be of four types:
first, there is the supernormal power as a result of karmic retribution (*vipākaja-abhijñā*), such as the five supernormal powers obtained as a reward by the various devas.
All such cases are included.
Second is the power of medicine:
as with the various rishis and others who, by the power of medicinal herbs, fly through the air with ease and mastery.
Third is supernatural power through incantations (*vidyā-siddhi*).
For example, there was a brahmin in Vārāṇasī who, by means of incantations, sustained his body and flew up to the celestial palaces.
He transformed his body into that of Śakra and engaged in sexual intercourse with the wife of Śakra’s husband.
Such as these are the supernormal powers of incantation.
Fourth are the supernormal powers of cultivation,
which are attained by practicing based on dhyāna.
Among these four, the first three are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
while the last one is indeterminate (*aniyata*).
According to the Abhidharma, those concerning the minds of others and recollection of past lives are invariably wholesome (*kuśala*).
The divine eye and divine ear are invariably indeterminate (avyākṛta).
The single type of supernormal power of the body is by nature wholesome (kuśala),
while the transformative mind that it produces is indeterminate.
Its essence consists of the mental factor of wisdom associated with the consciousness of others' minds and of recollecting past lives.
Because it coexists with meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), its nature is wholesome.
The divine eye and divine ear consist of the faculty of wisdom associated with the two consciousnesses of the eye and ear; taking supernormal power as their essence,
they do not coexist with meditative concentration,
and therefore their nature is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The essence of the supernormal power of the body is also a mental factor of wisdom associated with the mental consciousness and co-arising with a concentrated mind;
therefore, its nature is wholesome.
The transformative mind that arises from it is preceded by an intentional application of the mind (*manasikāra*) with the desire to perform various deeds.
However, that which arises is either a mind of its own level or a mind of another level;
it does not coexist with meditative concentration.
Therefore, their nature is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, all five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) have as their essence the mental application of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*) within the stage of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-bhūmi*),
and they all arise from a mind intent on benefiting sentient beings.
Therefore, their nature is entirely wholesome.
Even the mind of transformation arises with the intention to benefit sentient beings;
therefore, its nature is also wholesome.
The Mahāyāna teaches that the five mundane supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) are largely the same as those in the Abhidharma; thus,
the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* explains the meditative concentration of the transformation of the unconditioned (*avyākṛta-nirmāṇa-dhyāna*).
The five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) accomplished by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have true wisdom as their essence;
even the various transformations they manifest do not depart from meditative concentration (samādhi),
for they all arise through the power of the gateways of samādhi.
Their essential nature is entirely wholesome.
Such are the three natures.
Next, there is the sixfold classification of the three types of action (*karman*).
The actions of body, speech, and mind constitute these three types of karma.
When their essential nature is investigated, all six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) take wisdom as their substance.
Since this wisdom resides within the internal mind, it is of the nature of mental karma (manaskarma).
Regarding the inclusion of the three types of karma within the *Anusāralakṣaṇa-śāstra*, it is as explained in the *Di-lun* (*Dilun*):
first, the supernormal power of the body,
which is the purity of bodily action (*kāyakarma*).
The divine ear and the knowledge of others' minds purify the karma of speech;
the recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows purify the karma of mind.
Among these, the single supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows is not analyzed in that treatise.
The single type of supernormal power of the body consists of transformations within form;
therefore, it is called the purity of bodily action (*kāyakarma-viśuddhi*).
The divine ear and knowledge of others' minds arise based upon this.
Therefore, it is called purity of verbal action.
How does one initiate speech?
By means of the divine ear, one listens to and receives the true Dharma from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, they hear the various voices and languages of sentient beings and give teachings based upon them;
by means of the knowledge of others' minds, they understand the mental inclinations of beings.
It arises in accordance with that [knowledge].
Because these two supernormal knowledges are predominant within the arising of speech,
the treatise describes them as the purity of vocal action (*vākkarman*).
Through the supernormal powers of recollecting past lives and the divine eye, one thoroughly knows the events of the past and future.
Although the past and future are separated by vast intervals of time and difficult to know,
they are not beyond the scope of the mind’s comprehension.
Therefore, it is called the purity of mental action (*manas-karman*).
