Within the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-abhijñā*), one’s own realization of the destruction of the outflows and the internal freedom from defilement also constitute the purity of mental action.
To know the destruction of the outflows in others is what is termed "the destruction of the outflows."
This is the knowledge of whether the afflictions in the minds of other sentient beings have been exhausted or not;
based upon this, one gives rise to speech.
It resembles the supernormal power of knowing others' minds and is also a purity of vocal karma.
The three types of karma are thus.
Next, the seventh section clearly demonstrates the manifestation of the three kinds of discrimination,
as explained in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
All six are pervasive because they are unobstructed;
however, there is a distinction between "manifesting" (míng) and "demonstrating" (shìxiàn) in terms of their being hidden or revealed.
Distinguish this by means of four propositions:
first, that which is a manifestation but not an illumination,
namely, the supernormal power of the body and the knowledge of others' minds.
These two supernormal powers benefit sentient beings through transformation;
because they give rise to faith and manifest clearly,
they are called "manifestations."
Because it cannot eliminate or distance oneself from the three types of delusion,
it is not called "clarity.
These three delusions are as described below.
The second is clarity but not manifestation.

This refers to the divine eye and the supernormal power of recollecting past lives: the supernormal power of recollecting past lives eliminates ignorance regarding the prior limit [of existence], while the divine eye eliminates ignorance regarding the subsequent limit.
Therefore, it is called "illumination.
Because it generates faith in sentient beings through transformation without being extremely explicit,
it is not a "manifestation."
Why is it not manifest?
Because through the knowledge of past lives, he knows the events of his previous existences;
by recounting these past events, he transforms and benefits sentient beings.
Events separated by lifetimes are difficult to know;
most people do not believe them.
Therefore, these are not mere displays.
With the divine eye, he knows the affairs of future lives;
he speaks of future events to transform and benefit sentient beings,
for matters separated by lifetimes are difficult to know.
People likewise do not believe it;
therefore, it is not a manifestation.
The third [case] also clarifies that it is indeed a manifestation.

This refers to the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*). It is called "clarity" (*vidyā*) because it thoroughly penetrates the true truths, realizes the exhaustion of the outflows,
and thereby eliminates delusion regarding those true truths.
Knowing the exhaustion of others' outflows,
he discerns whether the afflictions within the minds of those sentient beings have been exhausted or not, and exhorts and transforms them;
they then give rise to faith.
It is called "manifestation" because it gives rise to faith and makes things clearly evident.
The fourth is neither clarity nor manifestation;
this refers to the supernormal power of the divine ear.
Because it cannot eliminate the three preceding types of delusion,
it cannot be called "clarity" (vidyā). Consequently,
its ability to transform others and inspire faith is not manifested.
Therefore, it is not a manifestation. Why is it not manifest?
Although the divine ear can hear distant sounds, it cannot communicate them to others by means of speech.
Others do not hear it and for the most part do not believe or accept it;
therefore, it is said to be "unmanifested.
Furthermore, it is established as a secret teaching for those disciples who are to be converted, spoken in private and at a distance.
Yet, when wishing to transform others, they claim that [the teaching] was transmitted from another and not through their own power;
thus, many do not believe it.
Such is the manner in which clarity and manifestation, as well as concealment and disappearance, occur.
When discussed comprehensively, they are all manifestations of clarity.
Therefore, within the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are distinguished and expanded into ten clarities (*daśavidyā*),
which are likewise fully manifested.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest these virtues in order to transform sentient beings.
A question is asked:
"The *Sūtra on Past Lives, the Divine Eye, and the Exhaustion of Outflows* states that these are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)."
Furthermore, it is also called "illumination" (vidyā) and "the three types of penetration" (traividya).
What is the difference between them?
The general explanation of their meanings is identical;
however, within this, there are differences when they are distinguished specifically.
What are these distinct characteristics?
As Nāgārjuna said:
"Directly knowing the eight kinds of past events and so forth is called the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
Among these, one knows karma and its fruits regarding the past."
The principle of causal conditions is called the clear knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-vidyā*).
Knowing that one dies here and is born there in future lives is called the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*).
Knowing karma and its fruits through the principle of causal conditions is called the clear knowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-vidyā*).

Directly knowing the exhaustion of the outflows is called the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*). Knowing that they will not arise again is called the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vidyā*).
Furthermore, knowing that cessation is attained through the Path and is distinct [from other forms of cessation] is also termed "clear knowledge."
To know such things exhaustively is called the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividya*).
This "exhaustiveness" has four levels. The first is the knowledge of phenomena (*vastujñāna*).
There is nothing regarding non-action that he does not know.
Second, he knows the principles and meanings of the phenomena of cause and effect;
there is nothing regarding their meaning that he does not know.
Third, knowing that the principle of the emptiness of the true truths is identical;
exhausting all characteristics to find them entirely empty.
Fourth, knowing their nature.
To fully know that all such phenomena arise from the *tathāgatagarbha* as their fundamental nature, and that their characteristics are themselves reality—
to exhaustively penetrate this is called the "threefold penetration" (*trividha-pratisaṃvid*).
This discussion applies to those common to ordinary beings, with the sole exception of the penetration of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
The clarity shared with the two vehicles is understood as being solely [the domain] of the Tathāgata; thus,
the manifestation of thorough clarity and discernment is explained.
Next, the eighth section clarifies the meaning of the sequential order for cultivating the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
In reality, there is no fixed sequence for the six supernormal powers;
however, for the time being, we shall speak of three types of sequence.
First, regarding the sequence of cultivation and realization:
according to the Buddha’s own account, as the Buddha was about to attain enlightenment,
Māra Pāpīyān came to disturb and confuse him out of fear that the Buddha would achieve the Way.
At that time, the Tathāgata must employ his supernormal powers to subdue them;
for this reason, he first cultivates the supernormal power of the body.
Once Māra has been subdued, [the task is accomplished].
He became invisible in mid-air;
at that time, the Tathāgata did not know his whereabouts and had to employ the divine eye to discern where he was.
Therefore, next, one cultivates the second [supernormal power], the arising of the divine eye.
Although the eye sees forms, it does not understand their speech;
thus, one must employ the divine ear to hear what is said.
Therefore, one next cultivates the third [supernormal power], the divine ear.
Although the ear hears their words, it does not fathom their minds;
one does not know whether their inner hearts are timid or courageous.
Therefore, one next cultivates the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others in sequence.
By means of this power, one knows that their inner mind is agitated, terrified, and uneasy;
yet, while knowing the present state of mind, one does not know the extent of their past merit.
"If this merit surpasses mine, it may create an obstacle and hinder my attainment of the Way.
To understand the past merits [of the Māra], he next cultivated the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
He saw that because of the Māra’s past performance of a single great unobstructed assembly (*mahāpariṣad*), he was now receiving this retribution.

"In the past, throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, for the sake of all sentient beings, I have sacrificed my body, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, and brain, undergoing various kinds of suffering; my merit surpasses theirs.
Knowing that it surpasses theirs, I do not fear their obstacles."
One is then able to sever the fetters and realize the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Therefore, next, the sixth supernormal power, the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, is explained.
Furthermore, Nāgārjuna says:
During the first watch of the night, the Buddha attained one supernatural power (*abhijñā*) and one clear vision (*vidyā*).
What is called "one supernatural power" refers to attaining the supernormal power of the body (*ṛddhi-vidhijñāna*);
what is called "one clear vision" refers to attaining the clear vision of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
During the middle watch of the night, he attained one supernormal power and one clear vision.
Regarding "one supernormal power," it refers to attaining the supernormal power of the divine ear.
Regarding "one clear vision," it refers to attaining the clear vision of the divine eye.
During the latter part of the night, he attained one supernormal power and one clear knowledge.

Regarding "one supernormal power," it refers to the attainment of the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others. Regarding "one clear knowledge," it refers to the attainment of the clear knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*).
For what reason does one first attain the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and subsequently attain the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*)?
The treatise itself explains:
"One seeks the three types of clear knowledge from among the six supernormal powers."
Because the power of maintaining [the practice] is weighty, one first attains the supernormal powers (abhijñā) and subsequently attains the clear knowledges (vidyā).
Question: Why is the sequence such?
The commentary’s own explanation states:
"At the beginning of the night, Māra came, wishing to cause disturbance;
in order to subdue him, [the Buddha] first manifested the supernormal power of rising from his seat."
Having subdued the Māras, he immediately reflected to himself:
"By what causes and conditions have I attained such great power within this single body?
He then sought out his past causes and saw that by having extensively cultivated merit and goodness in the past, he had obtained such power.
Thus, he gave rise to the recollection of his past lives.
At midnight, when the Māras had departed and all was silent and still,
the Buddha then compassionately contemplated all sentient beings.
I sought the divine ear because I wished to hear their words;

having attained the divine ear, I heard the sounds of suffering and joy of sentient beings throughout the five realms of existence in the ten directions, and I sought the divine eye because I wished to see their forms.
During the final watch of the night, desiring to know the minds of beings in order to teach and transform them accordingly,
he sought knowledge of the minds of others;
he perceived that all sentient beings desire to be free from suffering and seek happiness.
Since I have not yet attained the bliss of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), no one can bestow it upon me;
therefore, I seek the exhaustion of outflows.
This, too, is the sequence for its cultivation and accomplishment.
The first point is thus.
The second clarifies the sequence of cultivation and realization,
which is also based on the Buddha’s teaching.
As explained in the Vinaya:
at the first watch of the night, the Buddha attained the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives,
free from ignorance.
When darkness is exhausted, clarity arises; when darkness is exhausted, light arises.
At the time of midnight, one attains the clarity of the divine eye.
With the exhaustion of ignorance, clarity arises;
with the exhaustion of darkness, light arises.
During the final watch of the night, he attained the clarity of the destruction of the outflows.
Ignorance is exhausted and clarity arises;
darkness is exhausted and light arises.
These three constitute the sequence of cultivation and realization.
Having attained the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), one desires to transform sentient beings;
yet, not knowing which sentient beings require transformation,
one must employ the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*) to hear the sounds of the suffering and happiness of all sentient beings.
Next, he arouses the divine ear.
Although he knows the distinctions between the suffering and happiness of sentient beings, they are separated by spatial distance, making it difficult for him to go and transform them;
therefore, he next arouses the supernormal power of the body.
Even if one reaches a state that is unknown or undesired by them,
it is not appropriate to bestow the Dharma;
next, one should arouse the knowledge of others' minds.
Regarding these three subsequent types of the sequence for manifesting emanations,
the third directly clarifies the sequence for manifesting emanations;
this too is based on the Buddha’s teaching.
When wishing to transform others, if one does not know their location, one first employs the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Once their location is seen, one must go to guide and transform them;
for this, one next employs the supernormal power of the body (*ṛddhividhi*).
Having arrived at their location, he did not understand their speech;
next, he employed the divine ear,
yet although he understood their speech, he did not recognize their underlying faculties.
Next, one employs the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
Although one perceives the magnitude of their past faculties and dispositions, even if one recognizes those past roots, one does not yet know their present desires.
Next, one employs the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Although one knows their mind, one does not yet know whether afflictions exist within that mind.
Next, one employs the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna) to observe whether afflictions exist within the mind.
He teaches the remedies for them,
causing them to realize the exhaustion of outflows;
the sequence is as follows.
Next, the ninth section distinguishes the characteristics based on the sūtras,
as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
there are two types of supernormal power of the body (*kāyābhijñā*).
First is transformation (*pariṇāma*), second is metamorphosis (*nirmāṇa*).
To alter and replace an existing substance is called transformation.
There is no phenomenon that does not manifest as a teaching for the purpose of transformation.
These transformations are of many kinds, yet they are essentially sixteenfold.
The first is "earthquake" (trembling).
That is to say, they are able to shake a single world-system;
second, they cause fire to issue from the upper part of their bodies and water to issue from the lower part of their bodies.
Such are these [powers].
Third, filling the body with the emission of light that fills the world.
Fourth, manifesting.
For the sake of the assembly of all śramaṇas,
he performed five transformations into a different state,
changing the earth into water.
Sixth, water acts as fire and so forth;
sixth, coming and going, pervading and circulating, moving back and forth without obstruction or hindrance;
seventh, being large or small.
Transforming the small into the large,
and transforming the large into the small;
causing the eight kinds of colored forms to enter one's body.
They cause all sentient beings in all realms to enter their own bodies.
Ninth, regarding the similarity of where they go:
wherever they may travel, they manifest in a form identical to those sentient beings.
Their voices and speech are entirely identical to those [of ordinary beings].
Tenth is concealment and manifestation,
such as appearing and then disappearing, and so forth.
Eleventh, mastery:
being able to cause sentient beings to come, go, stay, or lie down entirely according to one's own will.
Twelfth, obstructing the supernatural powers of others.
Except for those mentioned above and their equals, it can entirely obstruct and obscure them.
Thirteenth, to sentient beings who lack eloquence, it can grant eloquence.
Fourteenth, to sentient beings who have lost mindfulness, it can grant right mindfulness.
Fifteenth, he can bestow happiness upon sentient beings who lack it.
Sixteenth, his body emits light that shines universally upon all things.
Such is the meaning of the transformation.
These emanations are also immeasurable,
yet they can be summarized into three types.
The first is the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
First, transforming into the forms and types of all sentient beings;
second, transforming speech,
manifesting as various sounds, voices, and languages.
Third, the sphere of transformation (*nirmāṇa-viṣaya*).
This refers to the transformation into all manner of things such as food and drink.
Within these transformed bodies, there are briefly five types.
First, transforming into something resembling one's own body;
second, transforming into something dissimilar;
third, transforming into the body of another.
Fourth, dissimilarity;
fifth, the manifestation of all transformations as similar or dissimilar within one's own body and the bodies of others.
There are seven types of manifested speech.
First, when preaching the Dharma with a wondrous voice, its sound is subtle and exquisite.
Second, when preaching the Dharma with a pervasive voice, the sounds produced are heard everywhere by all.
Third, speech arises from one's own body as a transformation, appearing as if it were emerging directly from the body.
Fourth, arising from the bodies of others, manifesting speech that appears to originate from them;
fifth, arising from nowhere at all;
sixth, preaching the True Dharma.
Seventh is the speech that instructs, reprimands, and transforms according to the specific circumstances.
Thus, within the sphere of such transformation, the activities performed are immeasurable;
such is the power of physical supernormal knowledge (*ṛddhi*).
The divine eye is of two kinds:
first, seeing forms and images of the present;
second, seeing death here and rebirth there in the future.
Within the supernormal power of the divine ear, one hears all sounds of sentient beings throughout the six realms of existence—
whether the voices of the noble or the non-noble, coarse or subtle, distinct or indistinct, emanated or non-emanated, distant or near— all of them without exception.
Within the supernormal power of knowing others' minds, one knows all the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings exactly as they are.
Question: Does this supernormal power directly know the mind?
One also knows the object of cognition (*ālambana*).
According to the Abhidharma, one knows only the other's mind but does not know its object;
however, if one knows the object, then the preceding person’s mental attention (*manasikāra*) takes my own mind as its focal point.
If I were to take that [other] mind as my object, I would incur the fault of my own mind transforming and reflecting upon itself.
Therefore, one only knows the [other's] mind and does not know its object.
However, according to the *Tattvasiddhi*, when correctly knowing another's mind, one also knows its object.
The Mahāyāna is likewise.
Even if the mind takes itself as its object, what fault is there?
Within the supernormal knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*), there are six distinctions.
First, one knows one's own past lives.
One knows eight kinds of matters concerning one's own past, and so forth.
What are these eight matters?
First, such names;
second, such natures;
third, such births.
4. Such food and drink;
5. such suffering and pleasure; 6. such longevity.
Seventh, such long duration;
eighth, such limit of lifespan.
Having known these eight matters of the past, [he understands them].
The first is called self-knowledge;
the second is knowledge of others.
This consists of knowing the six types of common practices among other sentient beings.
What are the six aspects?
First, such a name;
second, such a nature.
Third, such is their birth;
fourth, such is their food and drink;
fifth, such are their virtues and evils.
Sixth is such a lifespan.
To know this matter of others is called "knowing others.
Third is causing other sentient beings to know their own past lives.
Fourth, causing other sentient beings to know their own past lives;
fifth, causing other sentient beings to know the past lives of others;
sixth, causing other sentient beings to mutually know one another’s past lives.
The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayābhijñā) is of two kinds:
first, the noble wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) that can exhaust all outflows, which is called the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows;
second, the knowledge that knows the exhaustion of outflows, which is called the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
Regarding the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*), there are four distinct meanings as explained in the *Bhūmivastu*:
first, knowing for oneself that the outflows are exhausted.
Second, he knows the exhaustion of the taints in others.
Third, he knows as they truly are, whether the means for the exhaustion of the taints have already arisen or have not yet arisen;
the Noble Path is the means for the exhaustion of the taints.
He knows, as they truly are, both the arising and the non-arising of the four kinds of overweening pride regarding the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
To claim that one has attained what one has not attained is called overweening pride (*abhimāna*).
The meaning of the six supernormal powers has been briefly distinguished in this manner.
